The Lagos State Safety Commission has raised concerns over drowning risks along the state’s extensive coastline and waterways, urging beach operators, schools, parents and residents to strengthen safety measures to prevent avoidable deaths, particularly among children and young people. The Commission said communities stretching from Victoria Island to Ajah and other coastal areas faced peculiar water-related safety challenges, making public education, swimming supervision and emergency response training critical to preventing drowning incidents. The Director-General of the Commission, Lanre Mojola, raised the concern on Wednesday during activities marking this year’s World Drowning Prevention Day at SOI Beach, Elegushi, Victoria Island, Lagos. In a statement obtained by The PUNCH, the Commission quoted Mojola as saying, “The geographical location of Lagos, with its extensive coastline and surrounding waterways, makes water safety education imperative.” Mojola warned that the state’s proximity to water bodies should not result in preventable loss of lives, stressing the need for residents, particularly children and young people, to understand the dangers associated with swimming and other water-related activities. According to him, the Commission assembled professionals with expertise in swimming, water safety and drowning prevention to educate participants on practical ways of avoiding accidents and responding to emergencies. He added that the programme included demonstrations of rescue techniques and first aid to equip participants with the knowledge required to respond appropriately when drowning incidents occurred. Earlier, the Head of the Events and Hospitality Department of the Commission, Olubunmi Jegede, said drowning prevention could not be left to government institutions or individual organisations alone. Meaningful progress can only be achieved through a coordinated approach involving all stakeholders.” Jegede identified the use of appropriate life jackets, avoiding swimming under the influence of alcohol and ensuring adequate supervision at beaches and other aquatic environments as essential preventive measures. She called for greater vigilance among beach users and operators, particularly in ensuring that appropriate safety precautions were observed before allowing people to engage in water activities. In a presentation titled ‘Water Safety and Drowning Prevention: Building a Culture of Responsibility Among Youths’, the Commission’s Director of Training and Sensitisation, Tosin Sobola, highlighted the causes of drowning and strategies for preventing incidents. Sobola stressed the need to cultivate responsible attitudes towards water activities, particularly among young people and adults who engage in recreational swimming. She urged participants to understand water-related hazards and observe established safety guidelines rather than underestimate the risks associated with aquatic environments. Another facilitator, Peter Nwoke, President of Train the Trainers, delivered a presentation titled ‘The 10 Seconds That Decide Life and Death’, highlighting the importance of prompt intervention during drowning emergencies. The programme, organised in conjunction with SOI Beach and ITEM 7 (Go), attracted safety professionals, youth corps members, water safety experts, students from public schools in Education District III and other stakeholders. The Commission said the engagement was part of efforts to promote continuous public sensitisation, practical safety education and collaboration among government agencies, schools, beach operators, safety professionals and residents to reduce drowning incidents across Lagos.
